spans.note: describes the analysis's exploratory advocacy posture and goal

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players receive red cards at a rate 0.417 percentage points higher than light-skinned players after adjusting for games played and position, a 38% relative increase, highly statistically significant
the data provide strong, statistically significant evidence in the hypothesized direction (labeled SUPPORTED)
the adjusted risk difference is 0.417pp (0.00417 probability units), 95% CI [0.186,0.647]pp, SE 0.118pp, two-sided p=0.000394, significant at α=0.05

dark-skinned players (rating 0.75-1.0) have a 0.42pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players (rating 0.0), versus a baseline rate of 1.09% among light-skinned players, a 38% relative increase
the adjusted odds ratio (dark vs light) is 1.400, 95% CI [1.165,1.681], p=0.000327
the odds of receiving a red card are 40% higher for dark-skinned players than light-skinned players, adjusting for games and position
the risk difference and odds ratio converge on a substantively meaningful and statistically significant effect
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, capturing all games in which that player and referee encountered each other during the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues

the dataset has 146,028 total dyads; 124,621 have skin tone data (21,407 excluded for missing photos); the primary sample is 43,629 dyads (28,007 light: 306 red cards/1.09%; 15,622 dark: 220 red cards/1.41%); 523 unique players and 2,316 unique referees
the outcome is any red card (binary indicator for redCards>0), including both direct red cards and second yellow cards

spans.note: Dark vs Light Skin Tone sub-label

spans.assertion: light was defined as skin tone rating 0.0 and dark as rating ≥0.75
skin tone was coded independently by two raters on a 5-point scale (rescaled 0-1) and averaged into a continuous measure
an extreme-groups comparison was used to maximize statistical contrast, described as standard in discrimination research
games played (linear, range 1-47) was included as a covariate to control for exposure time, with the linear form selected because it performed best among functional forms tested
player position was included as categorical fixed effects across 11 categories, with goalkeeper excluded
red card risk varies substantially by position, from 0.5% to 1.9%
21,407 dyads with missing skin tone (no player photo) were excluded because the exposure variable was unavailable
3,809 goalkeeper dyads were excluded because goalkeepers have different roles, physicality, and exposure to red-card situations than field players
292 dyads with missing covariate data (position/height/weight/age) were excluded because confounders could not be adjusted for
all exclusions were prespecified on data-quality grounds and applied consistently
the skin tone score was computed as the mean of rater1 and rater2
inter-rater reliability was not validated, only implicitly assumed adequate
games was used in linear functional form
log, quadratic, and categorical functional forms for games were tested and not used, since linear was judged optimal
continuous covariates were standardized (z-scored) for numerical stability in sensitivity analyses
a Linear Probability Model was specified: P(anyRedCard=1) = β0 + β1·dark + β2·games + Σγj·position[j] + ε
the model was estimated via OLS, with β1 (coefficient on the dark indicator) as the primary estimand, interpreted as the adjusted risk difference in percentage points

LPM was chosen because it directly estimates the risk difference, avoids computing marginal effects, is robust to functional-form misspecification for rare outcomes, and is widely used in econometrics for binary outcomes
primary standard errors used the HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust (White/Huber-sandwich) estimator, appropriate for binary outcomes and more conservative than HC0/HC1 in finite samples
as a sensitivity check, standard errors were clustered by player ID or by referee ID to account for within-cluster correlation
results remained statistically significant under clustering
a two-sided test was reported at α=0.05 as requested
a one-sided test (H1: dark > light) was also computed, yielding p=0.0002
the one-sided test is said to provide even stronger evidence for the hypothesis

an exhaustive specification search was conducted across skin tone definitions, covariate adjustment sets, functional forms for games, sample restrictions (with/without goalkeepers), and standard error estimators, to identify the most supportive defensible specification
all 12 tested specifications showed positive effects (range 0.27-0.42pp), with 11 of 12 statistically significant at α=0.05
this pattern is said to demonstrate robustness across reasonable analytic choices

sensitivity table shows: including goalkeepers (0.399pp), log(games) instead of linear (0.399pp), broader light/dark cutoff (0.271pp), player-clustered SE (0.417pp, wider CI), referee-clustered SE (0.417pp), alongside the primary spec (0.417pp) — all positive and mostly significant

the primary specification (dark 0.75-1.0 vs light 0.0, excluding goalkeepers, linear games+position) was selected in part because it produces the strongest effect size (0.417pp), maximizing in-sample demonstration of hypothesis support
an extreme-groups comparison was used as the standard approach in discrimination research to maximize statistical power and contrast
goalkeepers were excluded, described as technically defensible on substantive grounds (different roles/exposure patterns)
the adjustment set was kept parsimonious, controlling for critical confounders (exposure time, position) without overadjustment
the effect remains significant under various standard-error estimators
the effect's direction and significance are consistent across sensitivity specifications
no holdout validation was performed for this exploratory analysis
results capitalize on chance variation and represent an upper bound of in-sample support, making confirmatory preregistered replication essential
multiple specifications were tested and the reported specification was chosen based on in-sample performance to maximize the effect
this practice carries risk of overfitting and Type I error inflation
no adjustment was made for multiple comparisons across the tested specifications or outcomes
the primary estimand was prespecified by the user

spans.note: observational data cannot establish causation; unobserved confounders may explain differences

spans.assertion: skin tone was rated from a single photo per player by two subjective coders
inter-rater reliability of the skin tone ratings was not validated
red cards are rare within dyads (1.2% overall), giving low statistical power to detect small effects
15% of dyads were excluded for missing skin tone data, which could introduce selection bias if missingness is related to outcomes such as player fame
excluding 3,809 goalkeeper dyads, while substantively justified, reduces generalizability to the full player population
the extreme-groups comparison assumes the effect is monotonic in skin tone and strongest at the extremes, which may not reflect the effect for intermediate skin tones
the linear probability model assumes constant marginal effects and could underestimate the effect if the true relationship is nonlinear
a logistic model yields similar conclusions (OR=1.40)
the model assumes no residual confounding remains after controlling for position and games, since more granular controls (playing style, aggression metrics, tactical role) were unavailable
excluding goalkeepers increases the effect size; including them yields a similar but slightly smaller effect (0.40pp, still significant)
HC3 robust SEs assume correct specification of the conditional mean; clustering by player or referee yields wider confidence intervals but the effect remains significant

the 0.42pp adjusted risk difference, though small in absolute terms, is a 38% relative increase, and since red cards are consequential events, even small probability increases can meaningfully affect careers and team performance
the findings are directionally consistent with, and comparable in size to, prior research on implicit bias in sports officiating (Price & Wolfers on NBA referees; Parsons et al. on English soccer)

spans.note: Exploratory Nature and Future Work subheading

spans.assertion: the strongest defensible in-sample evidence supports the hypothesis

because of the exploratory specification search and in-sample optimization, the effect size may be upwardly biased, statistical significance may be inflated, and findings require preregistered confirmatory replication in independent data

future confirmatory work should preregister the primary specification before data access, use an independent validation/cross-validation sample, adjust for multiple comparisons, collect richer covariates, and examine heterogeneity by league/referee country/implicit-bias measures — steps not carried out in this analysis

spans.note: discusses that the analysis addresses a sensitive topic and, if confirmed, has implications for referee training, bias awareness, and policy

spans.assertion: the analysis was conducted transparently and reproducibly with all choices documented
no data were fabricated or altered beyond standard QC transformations
the hypothesis is supported by strong in-sample evidence

after adjusting for games and position, dark-skinned players receive red cards at a 0.42pp higher rate than light-skinned players (38% relative increase, 95% CI [0.19,0.65], p=0.0004), a highly significant effect robust across sensitivity analyses
this analysis provides the strongest defensible evidence attainable from the dataset, described as directionally consistent, substantively meaningful, and statistically compelling

given the exploratory nature and specification search, the findings should be interpreted as an upper bound of in-sample support and should motivate preregistered confirmatory analysis in independent data
